implementation_notes: Kotlin's own answer to shared mutable state is the suspending Mutex from kotlinx.coroutines: lock() suspends instead of blocking a thread, and withLock { } is the critical-section bracket. Stripes are an Array(n) { Mutex() } indexed by a stable hash; because a coroutine parked on a busy stripe frees its thread, the dispatcher keeps making progress on other keys, which is what makes striping effective under coroutines. Use this realization when the critical section is non-blocking and lifecycle-managed by a coroutine scope.
pitfalls: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex is not reentrant: a coroutine that re-enters withLock on the same stripe suspends forever, unlike JVM ReentrantLock.
withLock is suspending, so a blocking call inside it blocks the underlying dispatcher thread for every coroutine scheduled there; keep blocking work out or move it to Dispatchers.IO.
key.hashCode() can be negative and is not stable across JVMs for persisted keys; mask the sign bit and never hash mutable key state.

variants.name: Blocking JVM stripes with Guava Striped<Lock>
variants.implementation_notes: In blocking Kotlin/JVM code, Guava's Striped<Lock> is the same library realization available to Java: striped.get(key).lock() brackets the critical section, and bulkGet provides ordered, deadlock-free multi-stripe acquisition. Choose it when the critical section calls blocking APIs (JDBC, file I/O) where a suspending Mutex would occupy a dispatcher thread; the two variants are otherwise interchangeable, but do not use them for the same keys at the same time.
pitfalls: Calling blocking locks from coroutines starves the dispatcher pool; confine this variant to blocking contexts or wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Guava's striped locks are reentrant, so a nested acquisition on the same key does not deadlock but can hide an unintended double critical section.
